evidence.title: When RAG Chatbots Expose Their Backend: An Anonymized Case Study of Privacy and Security Risks in Patient-Facing Medical AI
evidence.outcome: Privacy and security failures in a deployed patient-facing chatbot that went unidentified before deployment
evidence.effect: Serious privacy and security failures were identified with standard browser tools, without specialist skills or authentication; the authors conclude independent review should be a prerequisite for deployment.
evidence.quote: Serious privacy and security failures in patient-facing RAG chatbots can be identified with standard browser tools, without specialist skills or authentication; independent review should be a prerequisite for deployment.
evidence.sample_unit: publicly accessible patient-facing RAG chatbot deployments

commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether documented privacy, security, and threat assessments before deployment reduce privacy or security failures in health care AI. One deployment study found serious failures in a live patient-facing chatbot using standard browser tools, which shows the hazard exists but does not show that assessments prevent it.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, so certainty is rated as no direct evidence. The single hazard study examined one publicly accessible retrieval-augmented chatbot and documents a problem rather than the effect of an assessment. The endorsements, mostly frameworks and commentaries, reflect expert agreement rather than measured outcomes.

In one deployed patient-facing chatbot, reviewers found serious privacy and security failures using standard browser tools, without specialist skills or authentication. This suggests such failures can pass through deployment unnoticed. The authors conclude that independent review should precede deployment, but the study did not test whether a pre-deployment assessment would have caught these failures.

Endorsers tie the practice to existing obligations. One commentary states that HIPAA requires regular risk assessment, and CHAI notes that the annual HIPAA Security Risk Assessment is a condition of federal funding for community health centers. FDA draft guidance asks device makers for a security use case view covering AI features. One commentary cites GDPR Article 35 data protection impact assessments.

Many community health centers already complete an annual HIPAA Security Risk Assessment, so adding AI systems to that process may reduce the added cost. No study reports staff time, cost, or a reassessment interval, so organizations would set cadence without outcome data. The hazard study suggests some failures are detectable with low-cost browser tools.

No test of the practice exists, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The hazard study did not report the population served. One commentary calls for data protection impact assessments of AI translation tools, which patients with limited English proficiency may rely on, but it offers no outcome data.

The hazard study found that failures in a patient-facing chatbot were visible to anyone with a browser, which may expose patient information and affect trust. Patients generally cannot inspect these systems themselves and depend on the organization's review. No study reports whether assessments change patient harm or trust.

commentary.research_gap: Studies should compare AI deployments with and without documented pre-deployment privacy, security, and threat assessments. They should measure vulnerabilities found before and after go-live, exposure and breach incidents, cost, staff time, and the reassessment interval at which new risks appear, and they should include safety-net and community health center settings.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, and the single hazard study did not report the population served. Organizations serving Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients therefore have no evidence on whether these assessments work in their settings, although community health centers already perform HIPAA security risk assessments that could be extended to AI systems.
